title: Budget Airlines' Rival Isn't Each Other, It's the Credit Card Business That Sells Miles
dek: Ultra-low-cost carriers built their business on rock-bottom fares, and now they're squeezed between the big airlines' Basic Economy and frequent-flyer credit cards — the latter makes travelers willing to pay $100 more just to earn points, turning price-sensitive customers into the least reliable customers of all.
why: 18 minutes to explain why an entire business model stops working: not because it was beaten by a cheaper rival, but because a more expensive rival used a loyalty system to intercept its customers.
who: Investors and founders looking at consumer and airline sectors, especially those concerned with whether a low-price strategy can hold up long term and how loyalty programs intercept price-sensitive customers.
skip: The passenger complaint bits at the start can be fast-forwarded, and the self-promotion at 6:07 about a previous M&A episode can be skipped.

points.h: What budget airlines sell is: you get what you pay for
points.body: The episode opens with a string of passenger complaints that define the category: trays too small to hold anything, water costs extra, seats have almost no padding, and after overbooking they randomly kick people off the plane. But precisely because the price is low enough, people who want to travel cheaply keep pouring into budget airlines. Allison Sider says the peak of this model was about ten to twelve years ago, when it looked like it would become the dominant business model, and the big airlines did feel they had to find a way to respond.

points.h: Frontier even changed its ticker to ULCC
points.body: Frontier is headquartered in Denver, with white fuselages and forest-green lettering, and a different animal on the tail of every plane. In the 2010s it went all in on the ultra-low-cost model, and its ticker symbol is literally ULCC (ultra-low-cost carrier), which in Allison's words is "how much they wanted to embody that business model and own that identity." It and Spirit have highly similar business models and shared roots. But Frontier's operations have long been rough, with on-time rates, cancellation rates, and involuntary denied boarding rates consistently at the bottom of the rankings.

points.h: Both mergers failed, and Spirit simply disappeared
points.body: In 2022 Frontier proposed acquiring Spirit, hoping to merge into a national budget airline that could take on the big four of Delta, United, American, and Southwest, with the two route networks complementary — Spirit leaning east, Frontier leaning west. But JetBlue bid higher, Spirit turned to JetBlue, and then a federal judge blocked the deal on antitrust grounds. In the end no one got Spirit; it went through multiple bankruptcies and shut down completely this year. Spirit's disappearance opened up market space for Frontier, and the company says it has benefited, but at the same time it ran into inflation, high jet fuel costs, and a fading of demand for cheap travel itself.

points.h: The big airlines copied budget airlines' playbook with Basic Economy
points.body: Delta, American, and United all rolled out Basic Economy — a fare class cheaper than the rest of the cabin with minimal service. The big airlines' approach was not to cut prices across the board, but to take a few seats, price them close to budget levels, and pair them with near-budget bare-bones service, such as no advance seat assignment. For consumers, that means getting the budget airline experience on the big airlines' routes and reliability. Allison says this is the bet most airlines are now making: people want a more premium experience and are willing to pay for it. Delta made this bet first fifteen years ago, wagering that "if you have the best product and the most reliable operation, people will come," and it has been very successful.

points.h: What really kills budget airlines is the frequent-flyer credit card
points.body: The other mechanism the big airlines use to keep customers is loyalty programs: co-branded credit cards mean travelers don't even compare prices. Allison's example is that someone who wants to earn miles or status might be willing to pay $100 more. That makes it extremely hard for Frontier to compete — its route options aren't as broad, and its loyalty program isn't as strong. Frontier's response has been to start selling bundled products (ticket plus bag plus seat selection), and soon it will add first class and onboard Wi-Fi. In other words, it is becoming more and more like an ordinary airline.

points.h: Frontier CEO: fix operations first, then talk about the rest
points.body: Frontier CEO Jimmy Dempsey told Allison that the company's future is bright but it must adapt to the environment — "customers are seeking a more premium product, and we are adapting to that." Some of the actions he listed are very basic: improve operations, be more reliable. Allison's reading is that reliability is the center that supports everything else: only when operations are reliable, not always delayed or canceled, and with enough flights for backup, does it make sense to invest in a loyalty program and credit card. Dempsey's line is to continue offering very low fares across the industry to get people on planes, while layering on premium products to improve the overall revenue mix, and to find the "right balance" in the coming year.

points.h: Southwest's hesitation exposes the real problem with this trend
points.body: Southwest is the pioneer of budget airlines, bringing cheap flying to America, and it operates with extreme simplicity — every plane the same, every seat the same, which for a long time was an operational advantage but also made it miss out on revenue, because there was nothing to sell to people who wanted to upgrade. Now Southwest is also torn over whether to pivot toward premium demand, and it ultimately decided to pivot. But Allison points out that there is simultaneously an affordability crisis in the US, so "whether consumers' willingness to pay more for expensive tickets and premium experiences can last" is a big question hanging over this premiumization trend for years, and it is also why Southwest hesitated in the first place.

points.h: Price-sensitive customers have been judged unreliable
points.body: Allison says that for a long time, if you were the cheapest in the industry, you almost couldn't lose, so the question is: is this a fundamental change in the business model, or just a moment in the economic cycle that will swing back in the next recession? She thinks it's still an open question. But airlines are forming a judgment: price-sensitive customers may not be that reliable; affluent customers who can keep swiping their cards even when the economy wobbles are better customers. The whole industry is reshaping itself to serve that person. For budget airlines, that means there may be room for only one national big player, and after Spirit's disappearance that spot looks like Frontier's, but it has to return to profitability, and it may no longer look like it used to.
